paper.citation: Gwyther K, Rice S, Purcell R, Pilkington V, Santesteban-Echarri O, Bailey A, Walton CC. Sleep interventions for performance, mood and sleep outcomes in athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychology of Sport & Exercise. 2022;58:102094.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined sleep interventions in athletes, identifying 27 studies (617 athletes; 16 controlled and 11 uncontrolled designs). Twelve controlled trials were pooled, and sleep interventions improved subjective sleep quality, sleepiness and negative affect but not subjective sleep duration, objective sleep measures or aerobic and anaerobic performance indices.
paper.tldr: Across controlled trials, sleep interventions improved athletes' subjective sleep quality, sleepiness and negative affect, but there was no clear effect on objective sleep or performance, and the underlying studies were of low methodological quality.
paper.methods: PRISMA-based systematic review (not pre-registered) of five databases searched to April 2020. Narrative synthesis covered all 27 studies, and random-effects meta-analysis of Hedges g was run on 12 controlled trials, with quality appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
paper.findings: Sleep interventions improved subjective sleep quality (g = 0.62, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.02), sleepiness (g = 0.81, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.30) and negative affect (g = 0.63, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.98). No effect was found on subjective sleep duration, objective sleep duration or sleep efficiency, or on aerobic or countermovement jump performance. Objective onset latency was not significant overall but improved after removing one heterogeneous study (g = 0.81).
paper.limitations: Included studies were small and often non-representative, with only two of 22 appraised studies reporting a power analysis and most controlled trials lacking adequate blinding or concealment. The review was not pre-registered, intervention types could not be analysed separately, no RCTs of sleep extension were identified, no para-athletes or athletes with diagnosed sleep disorders were studied, and female athletes were under-represented.
paper.practicalImplications: Sleep hygiene, assisted sleep and sleep extension may help athletes' subjective sleep and mood, but the authors advise against firm recommendations because of low study quality. Staff should not expect performance gains from these interventions on the current evidence. Strategy choice should account for travel, late matches and training load.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not show that sleep interventions improve athletic performance. Sleep hygiene, assisted sleep and sleep extension may support how athletes feel about their sleep and their mood, so they can be considered alongside schedule demands such as travel and late matches.
paper.rtp: The review did not examine injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or sleep requirements after injury.
